coherence.reasons: Both run a clean line from 'do not launch, fund software' through market, unit economics, cash and the alternative. Y's executive summary maps one-to-one onto its five sections, and every section claim is restated as a slide title. X's summary is equally clear but has small breaks: slide 6's title says the best case would 'at best break even' while its own figure is −$1.76 (break-even appears only after an added promotion cut), and the Zipcart and risk slides are not reflected in the summary. Y has its own strain: the governing thought leans on a software break-even claim carried by one assumption-heavy slide, and 'nearly double ARR' sits awkwardly beside its own late-stage figure. Net, Y's hierarchy is marginally tighter.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion (decline, scale software) and both check per-order economics, separate growth from profit, test the runway rule and define reopening conditions. X weighs the trade-offs more carefully. It tests the founders' strongest counter-evidence at both median and best-observed inputs, and concedes that pricing is the one lever with evidence behind it. Its reopening triggers are sharper: two consecutive quarters of positive contribution at a 1,400+ orders/day mid-size-city site, a fee test where volume holds, and funding that keeps runway. It also points to a capital-light route (a from-store module, proven first on a customer's site at no cost) and quantifies the rider-pay and channel-conflict risks. Y adds a direct answer to the investors' path-to-profitability objective, plus owners and timings, which is useful. But its first reopening condition (one customer site positive for one quarter) is looser, and it dismisses the Zipcart case rather than weighing it.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: −$6.17, −$1.76, −$12.57, +$2.02, about 6 months of runway, about 42% growth and −$18.2M for nine stores at the median. X goes further on the critical evidence with fewer stretches. It runs the Zipcart levers at median (−$1.05) and at best-observed inputs (+$3.97), adds a best-plus-2%-promotions case (−$0.08), and derives the 3.75 orders per rider-hour needed to break even before store cost. It also reconstructs the pop-up ramp (about 180 to 410 orders a day), sizes rider-pay sensitivity, and treats the 37-deal pipeline as an upper bound. Y's 28-month payback, which adjusts for 22% retention, is better than X's 19-order figure, and its $63.4 break-even order value is correct. But Y leans on weaker inferences. Its software break-even at $11M ARR assumes costs stay flat while ARR grows 2.6 times at a sustained 60%. 'Nearly double ARR' assumes all 37 deals close. It compares a 27% goods margin with an 81% software margin as like for like. It also asserts that density alone had not made the Zipcart city profitable, which the pack does not state. Y tests Zipcart's levers only at the median, so it misses that the economics do turn positive at best-observed density.

revision.reasons: Both correctly reject the founders' hypothesis while granting that growth is real. Both rebut the 'we run stores better' claim by noting the 14 benchmark sites already run on Parcelbird software. X updates more precisely. It shows the result both before and after store cost because the founders' 'contribution' is undefined, and it notes the plan survives missing any single target but not all four. It takes the Zipcart evidence as partial support: positive only with a fee at best-ever order value and density, which no site has shown. It then turns that into a specific reopening trigger. Y fairly notes that the Midwest claim cannot be tested and that the founders are right about demand. But it treats Zipcart mainly as a refutation ('pricing, not better operations') and does not acknowledge the conditions under which the founders' thesis could hold.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the board to the right decision with correct core arithmetic. X serves the decision maker somewhat better. It handles the founders' best counter-argument (Zipcart) fully and fairly, gives sharper and more testable reopening triggers, quantifies the secondary risks, and stays conservative on the software upside. Y's strengths are a tidier hierarchy, a better retention-adjusted payback, an explicit action plan with owners, and a direct attempt to answer the profitability objective. That attempt rests on an optimistic flat-cost, sustained-60%-growth model, and Y overstates the pipeline. A board with two founders in the room would find X's analysis harder to argue against.
